baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2024 interview on Mexican civil wars, Canadian confederation and American secession; continental linkage, not an exhaustive world history.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Taylor compares rival projects of union, liberal rights and sovereignty across North American polities.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2024 answers on Lincoln/Juárez and threats to union; describes a substantive political-history contribution without treating liberal ideals as universal outcomes.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Taylor criticizes the continued use of Turner’s racial and national types in Kluger’s expansion narrative, arguing for differentiated Indigenous and colonial histories (2008).
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own scholarly review paragraphs on Turner and Kluger, especially “Like Turner, Kluger insists” and the French-war comparison. The immediate object is Kluger’s recycled Turner; his attributed Limerick quotation is not assigned to Taylor as original wording. Book unread.

baseline_incident_edges.relationship: Wood questions Taylor’s treatment of captive violence and the narrative scale of The Divided Ground while praising its research and cultural analysis.
baseline_incident_edges.evidence_note: Own2006 review distinguishes omission criticism from praise of the murder-law analysis and research. Richter supplies Wood’s captive-treatment counterexample; the approved Richter→Wood resource is separately represented, not repeated. Richter’s unnamed study remains bibliographically unidentified. Taylor’s complete book and later2016/2021reviews unread; no general verdict on Native history adopted.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: History Workshop provides publication and teaching settings for oral-history practice
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Editorial synthesis supported by the listed bibliography; the specific relationship remains subject to passage-level review. Samuel’s 1976 article is checked at metadata level only. Becky Taylor’s firsthand recollection documents Anna Davin teaching oral history in 1998, supplying a concrete participant mechanism where the earlier link was generic. The full Samuel article remains unread. Selected primary reprint passages now support Samuel’s specific methodological intervention, including his refusal to treat oral testimony as sufficient by itself. Original-printing collation remains unperformed.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: offers historical resources that feminist historians extend while questioning their gendered limits
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Taylor describes a concrete feminist development of Thompson’s work. The connection concerns gender history, not every theory discussed in gender history.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Gender in the making of class: a women's town and a men's town, Paris and Hanover, Ontario (1985–90)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: In-period, her own words (Atlantis, 1985): 'students of men's work and men's participation in labour organisations', with women's historians and historians of childhood, 'have reified the skill-unskill boundary' (p. 42); 'Skill, too, is a socially constructed category' (pp. 42–43). Of the Marxist analysis in Women at Work, Ontario, 1850–1930 (1975) she writes, quoting feminist critics (n. 20: Phillips and Taylor; Hartmann), that it 'explains why a hierarchy of labour is necessary within the waged labour force, but tells us nothing about why women end up at the bottom of this hierarchy' (p. 43). The Gender of Breadwinners (1990; unread here) compares Paris and Hanover, Ontario. Heron, a labour historian, reviewing it (CHR, 1991, read in full): 'the most exhilarating, challenging book to appear in modern Canadian social history in many years'; it 'integrates and surpasses' women's, labour, technological and economic history, and 'Parr gives the boot to neo-classical analysis, simplistic Marxism, and radical feminism' (p. 218). He quotes its introduction that 'the parts and proportions of the social landscape covered by class and gender alter' (p. 10) but finds that in the 1949 Paris strike 'she has suppressed the impact of class where it was undeniably a crucial force' (p. 220). From her own figures he suggests that 'the portrait of the "women's town" may be slightly misleading' (p. 219). He also finds that she downplays the wars and the state and 'seldom makes any reference to the considerable Canadian literature on work, class, gender, or small-town life' (pp. 220–21). He concludes that she 'has pushed us onto new terrain where gender is neither ignored nor is it given a monocausal explanatory force' (p. 221). Scheinberg (Archivaria, 1991) sees 'a more dynamic alternative to the old and stale studies that focused more on workers' industrial and organizational activities', while doubting conclusions drawn from 'the testimony of seven women' (p. 175). Dennis (EcHR, 1991) calls it 'an important contribution to the literature of labour history and locality studies' (p. 762). A contribution from inside the field's gender strand, alongside Sangster (1989) and Bradbury (1993). It does not claim that labour history lacked gender before 1990. edge_842 and edge_889 (cdn_women_gender → cdn_working_class) already carry the entry-level contribution and critique.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Opens the debate: the 1982–83 Chartism essays and introduction, then 'The Determinist Fix' (1996) on the obstacles to the linguistic approach; Mayfield and Thorne (1992) and Lawrence and Taylor (1993) take his work as the case
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Kirk 1987, pp. 2–3 (read): the revisionists' claim that workers were less motivated by class than the Thompsons and Hobsbawm held, with Stedman Jones (1982, 1983) the most fully argued case; Eley and Nield 2000, p. 7 (read): his Chartism essay 'originally set the linguistic cat among the social history pigeons'. Mayfield and Thorne take him as 'the case' of the linguistic turn (1992, abstract read); the 1996 title states a residual determinism as the obstacle to the linguistic approach (unread). Strand from_experience_to_language_1963_83.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Met the linguistic turn by combining it with social evidence: the reply with Taylor in the Stedman Jones round (1993), the critique of 'electoral sociology' (1997, as quoted by LoPatin), Speaking for the People against 'the rise of class politics' (1998), and the insistence that 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches be combined (response posted 2010)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Speaking for the People, chapter openings read (via the chapter DOIs): 'Many of the historical certainties which once underpinned the notion of "the rise of class politics" have come into question over the last decade … the retreat from social explanation has by no means been as comprehensive as commentators sometimes suggest' (p. 41); the Cambridge description's challenge to 'the rise of class politics' and 'the triumph of party'. Lawrence's 2010 response to Vernon (read in full): combining 'realist' and 'constructivist' approaches is necessary; scepticism about social data is 'a counsel of despair'. The 1993 reply with Taylor is unread (title and metadata only); Party, State and Society known through LoPatin (1999, excerpt read). Drafting addition built from agent B's evidence (§§C1–C3, P5).

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Cooper's retrospective on Thompson (1995) and his 2000 reply brought African labour history — 'people struggling not to be a working class' — into the debate's last round
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Cooper 2000, read in full: 'As in Thompson's England, much of the story is about people struggling not to be a working class, struggles that were not without consequences' (p. 62); 'The Haitian revolution and controversies over slavery forced an empire-wide perspective into debates in Europe' (p. 63); n. 6 points to Decolonization and African Society (1996) 'for a fuller argument'. The 1995 Social History retrospective is unread (Taylor & Francis 403); Eley and Nield cite it (2000, n. 2; reply p. 82). Moderate.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Politics and the People (1993): between 1832 and 1867 'the official political subject was redefined in the image of print' and the public sphere narrowed, so that 'the invention of democracy in England was then a sham' (as quoted by Tilly, 1994); Re-reading the Constitution (1996) gathered the 'new cultural history of British politics' (his phrase, 2004)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Pp. 107 and 336 as quoted by Tilly (1994, read in full; the book unread): 'despite all the legislation which historians have traditionally seen as heralding a brave new world of mass democratic politics … this period witnessed a marked decline in people's ability to shape the political appeals available to them as the official political subject was redefined in the image of print'; 'The invention of democracy in England was then a sham'. Re-reading the Constitution: contents read (Epstein, Fulcher, Wahrman, Burney, Antony Taylor, Joyce, Clark). The phrase 'the new cultural history of British politics' from his 2004 review of Epstein (opening read). Eley and Nield (2000, p. 8, read) on his 'neglected traces'.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Requires comparative cultural inquiry to reconsider its own standards rather than predetermine equal evaluations of every cultural product.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Selected primary printed pp. 68–73. Equal dignity and openness to cultural value are distinguished from compulsory identical judgments. Taylor’s polemic against subjectivism is not adopted as a neutral description of Foucault, Derrida or multiculturalism as a whole.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Lawrence explicitly acknowledges Stedman Jones, his supervisor in the 1980s, as an enduring intellectual inspiration in Speaking for the People (1998).
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Lawrence’s own acknowledgments establish the mentoring debt. They also credit Miles Taylor, Jane Elliott and other readers; this does not assign the book’s arguments solely to his supervisor or settle the separate 1993 joint reply.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Lawrence and Miles Taylor criticize Languages of Class for neglecting reception, political contingency and social structure (1993).
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: A joint argument by both authors. Their main reply challenges Mayfield and Thorne; it also defends Jones against simple linguistic determinism. Selected primary transcription read, not facsimile-collated; distinct from Lawrence’s 1998 mentoring acknowledgment.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Thomas’s review identifies Taylor as a specific target of Pagden’s defense of Enlightenment cosmopolitanism against communitarian restrictions on moral judgment.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Explicitly mediated by Keith Thomas’s 2014 review of The Enlightenment: And Why It Still Matters (2013), in the paragraphs on communitarian adversaries. The localist and moral-relativist characterization is Pagden’s position as reported by Thomas, not an editorial judgment that it accurately exhausts Taylor’s philosophy. Alasdair MacIntyre retains co-target credit; no response by Taylor is inferred. Pagden’s original book and Taylor’s underlying works were not freshly read.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Wood uses Richter’s study of Iroquois captive warfare to question Taylor’s account of Native punishment and cross-cultural differences.
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Wood’s own2006 review expressly names Richter’s earlier study in the section2 discussion of captives. This records Wood’s specific scholarly use, not Richter’s endorsement of Wood’s criticism of Taylor. Richter’s1983 War and Culture is a bibliographic lead; Wood does not identify the title, and the match is unconfirmed. The article body and Taylor’s complete book remain unread; the detailed description is Wood’s account. Section1’s separate Facing East discussion and the later unnamed-anthropologists claim are not conflated.

relevant_group_routes.relationship: Challenges 'the now commonplace assumption' that the colonial relationship between Indigenous peoples and Canada 'can be reconciled via such a politics of recognition'; liberal recognition 'can subtly reproduce non-mutual and unfree relations' (2009)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Own words, PhD dissertation (2009), abstract p. iii and pp. 26–27 (the 'commonplace assumption' p. 26; 'can subtly reproduce non-mutual and unfree relations' p. 27), where Taylor's 'The Politics of Recognition' (pp. 32–33) is quoted as the influential statement to be challenged; the 2014 book's subtitle, 'Rejecting the Colonial Politics of Recognition' (publisher). The book itself is unread at first hand. relevant_group_routes.relationship: Finds 'the undertheorization of identity sitting at the heart of scholarship on the Canadian politics of recognition': Taylor's use of 'identity' conceals a tension between 'situated self-understanding' and 'official classification' (2014)
relevant_group_routes.evidence_note: Own words, 'Métis' (2014), introduction p. 14 (publisher sample, read), summarising chapter 5: two 'methodological shortcomings of Taylor's narrow use of identity': it 'marginalizes discussion of the extent to which the process of public recognition itself may prove constitutive to the claims of collective identity', and 'in positioning misrecognition as an external force, it overlooks how it also shapes the internal claims of the group'. Chapter 5 itself is unread. Distinct from Coulthard's critique of Taylor (edge_2132): Andersen keeps the concept of (mis)recognition (p. 20) and criticises Taylor's concept of identity.
